etymology: From Middle English broiden, to embroider or work with the needle (Old English bregdan, to weave, plait), rendering the Hebrew tashbets, a garment of chequered or cellular work. It names the woven coat of the priest, wrought of fine linen in a diaper pattern.
biblical_def: The broidered coat was one of the holy garments the LORD commanded for Aaron and his sons, named in the roll of priestly vesture: “a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle” (Exo 28:4). It was the innermost garment, worn next the flesh, wrought “of fine linen” and embroidered with the needle: “And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen” (Exo 28:39). The same broidered work clothes the LORD’s espoused people in the parable of Ezekiel, where He says, “I clothed thee also with broidered work” (Eze 16:10) — the naked and cast-out infant arrayed by grace in the garments of a queen. So the priest’s coat was no bare covering but a thing of costly, patient artistry, that they who drew near to a holy God might be clothed with beauty as well as with modesty. Herein is the gospel figured: the sinner comes naked, and is clothed not in the rags of his own weaving but in a righteousness woven for him and put upon him. “He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isa 61:10). The broidered coat preaches that the fine linen of the saints is the gift of God, embroidered by grace and worn before His face.
webster_summary: The embroidered inner coat of fine linen worn by the priests of Israel next the flesh.
webster_full: BROIDERED COAT, the embroidered tunic of fine linen worn by the priests of the sanctuary.
It was the innermost of the holy garments, put on next the flesh beneath the robe and ephod.
It was wrought with the needle in a chequered or cellular pattern of fine white linen.
The word broider is an older form of embroider, to work a figure upon cloth with the needle.
The same broidered work is used in Scripture as a figure of the raiment God bestows upon His people.

And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen, and thou shalt make the mitre of fine linen, and thou shalt make the girdle of needlework.
I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers’ skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: A garment of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the truth that the righteousness we wear before God is woven and given by Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The broidered coat rebukes the proud thought that a man may weave his own covering for the presence of God. The age loves the raiment of its own making — the self-fashioned goodness that is but the fig-leaf apron over again. But no needle of ours can embroider a coat fit for the holy place; the flesh next which it is worn is the very flesh that must be washed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the imputed and gifted nature of our covering. The priest did not sew his own coat; it was made for him by God’s command and put upon him. So the fine linen of the saints is a righteousness wrought by Another and bestowed by grace, that we might minister before the LORD clothed in beauty not our own.
roots_summary: The embroidered linen coat of the priest, figuring the given righteousness in which sinners are clothed before God.
roots_lines: Broidered coat — the priest’s embroidered inner tunic of fine linen (Exo 28:4).
It was wrought with the needle in chequered work and worn next the flesh (Exo 28:39).
The word broider is an older form of embroider, from Middle English broiden, to weave or plait.
The same broidered work clothes the LORD’s espoused people by grace (Eze 16:10).
It figures the garments of salvation which God Himself puts upon His own (Isa 61:10).
usage: The priest came before God not in his own weaving but in the broidered coat God commanded.
As the coat was embroidered with patient art, so grace clothes the naked sinner with beauty.
No man may sew for himself a broidered coat fit for the holy place.

etymology: From Old English brēc, plural of brōc, a garment for the loins, cognate with the Latin bracae. It renders the Hebrew miknac, from a root meaning to gather in or bind up, a covering drawn about the loins and thighs.
biblical_def: The breeches were the linen undergarment the LORD commanded for the priests, made expressly for modesty and covering: “And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness; from the loins even unto the thighs they shall reach” (Exo 28:42). They were of “fine twined linen” (Exo 39:28), worn upon the flesh beneath every other garment (Lev 6:10), and were among the holy garments the high priest put on for the great day of atonement: “he shall have the linen breeches upon his flesh” (Lev 16:4). Their whole office was to hide the shame of nakedness from the eyes of a holy God as the priest went up to the altar. Herein Scripture is tender and grave at once. Ever since Eden, nakedness has been the mark of guilt, and the first act of mercy was that God clothed our parents with coats of skins. The linen breeches carry that mercy into the sanctuary: no flesh may minister uncovered before the LORD. They teach that reverence begins in modesty, and that the servant who draws near must not presume upon God’s holiness by exposing what shame would hide. What the breeches did in figure, the righteousness of Christ does in truth, covering our nakedness that we may stand before the throne unashamed.
webster_summary: The linen undergarment worn by the priests upon the flesh, made to cover their nakedness before God.
webster_full: BREECHES, a garment for the loins and thighs; among the priests, the linen drawers worn next the flesh.
They were commanded to cover the nakedness of the priests as they ministered at the altar.
They reached from the loins even unto the thighs and were of fine twined linen.
They were the undermost of the holy garments, put on before all the rest.
The word is of Old English origin, brēc, a covering for the lower body.
scriptures: And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness ; from the loins even unto the thighs they shall reach:
And a mitre of fine linen, and goodly bonnets of fine linen, and linen breeches of fine twined linen,
Lev 6:10

And the priest shall put on his linen garment, and his linen breeches shall he put upon his flesh, and take up the ashes which the fire hath consumed with the burnt offering on the altar, and he shall put them beside the altar.
Lev 16:4

He shall put on the holy linen coat, and he shall have the linen breeches upon his flesh, and shall be girded with a linen girdle, and with the linen mitre shall he be attired: these are holy garments; therefore shall he wash his flesh in water, and so put them on.
corruption_summary: A garment of modesty, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the reverence and shame-covering that becomes those who draw near to a holy God.
corruption_paragraphs: The linen breeches rebuke an age that has cast off shame and made the uncovering of the flesh a boast. Scripture treats nakedness as the token of guilt to be hidden, not flaunted; and it will not suffer even the priest to approach the altar uncovered. Where modesty is mocked as prudery and exposure is called freedom, this small commandment stands as a quiet reproof of the whole spirit of the age.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reverence begins in the covering of shame. From the coats of skins in Eden to the linen breeches of the priest, God has clothed the nakedness of sinners; and He requires that those who come near Him come covered. What the breeches figured, the righteousness of Christ fulfils, hiding our shame that we might stand unashamed before Him.
roots_summary: The priest’s linen undergarment of modesty, covering the nakedness of the servant who draws near to God.
roots_lines: Breeches — the priest’s linen drawers, worn next the flesh (Exo 28:42).
They were made to cover nakedness, reaching from the loins unto the thighs.
They were of fine twined linen, the undermost of the holy garments (Exo 39:28).
The word is Old English brēc, a covering for the lower body.
They figure the covering of shame that reverence before God requires (Lev 16:4).
usage: No flesh might minister uncovered; the priest first put on his linen breeches.
As Eden’s coats of skins hid the shame of guilt, so the breeches hid the priest’s nakedness at the altar.
Modesty before the holy God is not prudery but reverence commanded.

etymology: Bell is from Old English belle, a hollow sounding vessel; the golden bells (Hebrew pa’amon, from a root meaning to strike or ring) alternated on the hem of the high priest’s robe with worked pomegranates (Hebrew rimmon) of blue, purple, and scarlet.
biblical_def: Upon the hem of the high priest’s blue robe the LORD set an ordered fringe of golden bells and coloured pomegranates: “And beneath upon the hem of it thou shalt make pomegranates of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, round about the hem thereof; and bells of gold between them round about” (Exo 28:33). They were set in strict alternation, “A golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, upon the hem of the robe round about” (Exo 28:34), and so the workmen made them of pure gold (Exo 39:25-26). The bells were not ornament only; they were a sound of life. As Aaron went in unto the holy place before the LORD and came out again, the ringing was heard, “that he die not” (Exo 28:35) — a witness that the mediator lived and moved in the presence of God on the people’s behalf. The pomegranate, laden with seed, spoke of fruitfulness; the bell, of testimony. Together they preach the living Mediator: our great High Priest is passed into the heavens, and the sound of His intercession is never silent. So long as the bell is heard, the people without know that One appears for them in the presence of God, and that His work bears fruit unto the Father. Distinct from the mere fruit of the orchard, these are the holy hem-ornaments of the man who bore Israel before the mercy-seat.
webster_summary: The alternating golden bells and coloured pomegranates set round the hem of the high priest’s robe.
webster_full: BELLS AND POMEGRANATES, the ornaments of gold and coloured yarn set upon the hem of the high priest’s robe.
The bells were of pure gold; the pomegranates were wrought of blue, purple, and scarlet.
They were placed in alternation, a bell and a pomegranate, round about the whole hem.
The bells sounded as the high priest went into and came out of the holy place, that he die not.
They are distinct from the pomegranate as a fruit; here the word names an ornament of the priestly vesture.

A golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, upon the hem of the robe round about.

A bell and a pomegranate, a bell and a pomegranate, round about the hem of the robe to minister in; as the LORD commanded Moses.
corruption_summary: An ornament of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the witness of a living Mediator ever heard in the presence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The golden bell rebukes a silent and forgetful profession. The age hears no sound from the holy place and presumes there is no Mediator there; it lives as though the heavens were empty and the throne unattended. But the bell teaches that the going in and coming out of the great High Priest is a matter of life and death for the people, and that His voice on our behalf is never still.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the living and unceasing intercession of Christ. The bell was heard that Aaron die not; so the church without hears, by faith, the sound of her High Priest who ever liveth to make intercession. The pomegranate, full of seed, adds that His mediation is fruitful, bearing His people up to God.
roots_summary: The golden bells and coloured pomegranates of the high priest’s hem, witness of the living and fruitful Mediator.
roots_lines: Bells and pomegranates — the alternating ornaments on the hem of the high priest’s robe (Exo 28:33).
The bells were of pure gold; the pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet (Exo 39:25).
The bells sounded as the priest went in and out, that he die not (Exo 28:35).
The bell speaks of testimony; the pomegranate, laden with seed, of fruitfulness.

usage: The people heard the golden bell and knew their mediator yet lived before the LORD.
As bell alternated with pomegranate, so testimony joins with fruitfulness in a true priesthood.
Our High Priest is entered into the heavens, and the sound of His intercession is never hushed.

etymology: From Old French pomel, a little apple or rounded knob (Latin pomum, an apple), rendering the Hebrew gullah, a bowl or rounded basin. It names the swelling globe-like tops set upon the two brazen pillars of Solomon’s temple.
biblical_def: The pommels were the rounded, bowl-like crowns wrought atop the two great pillars, Jachin and Boaz, that stood before Solomon’s temple. In the temple record they are named among Huram’s brass work: “the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters” (2Ch 4:12). Four hundred pomegranates were set on the wreaths that covered them (2Ch 4:13), and the same objects are called “the two bowls of the chapiters” in the parallel account (1Ki 7:41-42). A pommel was thus the swelling globe upon the pillar-head, a rounded ornament of cast brass, crowned and netted and hung with pomegranates. Small as the word is, it belongs to the careful record of a house built wholly by pattern, where nothing was left to the workman’s fancy but all was made as the LORD had shown. The two pillars stood as pledges of establishment — Jachin, “He shall establish,” and Boaz, “In it is strength” — and their crowning pommels were the finished ornament of that stability. So the Scripture stoops to name the very knops and bowls of God’s house, that we might learn how exact and how beautiful is the order of the temple He builds, and how He crowns His pillars with comeliness as well as strength.
webster_summary: The rounded, bowl-shaped ornaments crowning the tops of the two brazen pillars of Solomon’s temple.
webster_full: POMMELS, the rounded knobs or globes set upon the chapiters of the two pillars before Solomon’s temple.
They are also called the bowls of the chapiters in the parallel record of the Kings.
They were of cast brass, covered with wreaths or networks and hung with pomegranates.
The word comes from the Old French for a little apple, a swelling rounded top.
They belonged to the ornamental crowning of the pillars Jachin and Boaz.
scriptures: To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars;
And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars.
The two pillars, and the two bowls of the chapiters that were on the top of the two pillars; and the two networks, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars;
And four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, even two rows of pomegranates for one network, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters that were upon the pillars;
corruption_summary: An ornament of the temple, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the exactness and comeliness of the house God builds by pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: The pommels rebuke the careless spirit that despises detail in the worship and house of God. The age counts such things trifling — a knob upon a pillar, a bowl of brass — and would build the church by its own convenience rather than by the given pattern. But the Scripture that names the pommels teaches that God is not indifferent to the fashion of His house, and that beauty and order there are matters of His own command.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God builds by exact pattern and crowns His pillars with comeliness. The two pillars pledged establishment and strength; their rounded pommels were the finished ornament of that stability. So in the true temple, Christ’s church, He joins strength to beauty and leaves nothing to the fancy of men.
roots_summary: The rounded bowl-like crowns of the temple pillars, ornament of a house built wholly by God’s pattern.
roots_lines: Pommels — the rounded globe-like tops of the two brazen pillars of the temple (2Ch 4:12).
They are called the bowls of the chapiters in the parallel account (1Ki 7:41).
The word is from Old French pomel, a little apple or rounded knob.
They were covered with wreaths and hung with four hundred pomegranates (2Ch 4:13).
They crowned the pillars Jachin and Boaz, pledges of establishment and strength.
usage: Even the pommels of the pillars were made by the pattern God showed, not the workman’s fancy.
God crowned His pillars with comeliness as well as strength.
Scripture stoops to name the knops and bowls of His house, that we learn its exact order.

etymology: Caul is from the Old French cale, a covering or membrane, rendering the Hebrew yothereth, an appendage or lobe. It names the fatty membrane or lobe upon the liver, burnt with the fat upon the altar; not the women’s netted headdress of Isaiah 3.
biblical_def: The caul of the liver was the fatty membrane or lobe lying above the liver, singled out by the LORD to be taken with the fat and the kidneys and burnt upon the altar in every offering. At Aaron’s consecration it is named: “the caul that is above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them” (Exo 29:13). It recurs through the law of sacrifice — in the peace offering, “the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away” (Lev 3:4, 3:10) — and in the sin offering Aaron “burnt upon the altar” the fat, the kidneys, and the caul above the liver (Lev 9:10). These innermost and richest parts, hidden deep within the beast, were the LORD’s portion, reserved wholly for Him and consumed in the fire of the altar. Herein is a searching lesson. God claimed not merely the outward flesh but the inward fat, the choicest and most secret part; He would have the best, and He would have the inmost. So He requires of His people not the surface of religion but the hidden man of the heart, the inward parts given up to Him. What the caul figured in the beast, the whole devotion of the soul must render in the worshipper: the deepest and richest of us laid upon the altar and offered up to God.
webster_summary: The fatty membrane or lobe above the liver, taken with the fat and burnt upon the altar in the offerings.
webster_full: CAUL OF THE LIVER, the fatty membrane or lobe lying upon the liver of a sacrificial beast.
It was taken away with the fat and the two kidneys and burnt upon the altar.
It is named in the consecration offering and throughout the law of the offerings.
The Hebrew doctors take it for the midriff or the lobe appended to the liver.
It is distinct from the caul as a woman’s netted headdress named in Isaiah’s reproof.

Lev 3:4

Lev 3:10
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Lev 9:10
But the fat, and the kidneys, and the caul above the liver of the sin offering, he burnt upon the altar; as the LORD commanded Moses.
corruption_summary: A part of the offering, not a contested doctrine; it recovers God’s claim upon the inmost and best of the worshipper.
corruption_paragraphs: The caul of the liver rebukes a religion of the surface that gives God the outward flesh and keeps back the hidden fat. The age offers Him its spare hours and its public shows, but reserves the inmost heart for itself. The law that claimed the caul and the kidneys — the deepest and richest parts — testifies that God will not be served with the outside only, but requires the secret man within.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD claims the inmost and the best. The fat and the caul, hidden deep within the beast, were burnt wholly to Him; so He asks of us the hidden man of the heart, the choicest of our love laid upon the altar. It is distinct from the cauls, the women’s headdress of Isaiah’s day.
roots_summary: The fatty lobe above the liver, the LORD’s inward portion in the offering, figuring the surrender of the inmost heart.
roots_lines: Caul of the liver — the fatty membrane above the liver, burnt with the fat and kidneys (Exo 29:13).
It recurs through the law of the peace and sin offerings (Lev 3:4; Lev 9:10).
The word caul is from Old French cale, a covering or membrane.
These innermost, richest parts were reserved wholly as the LORD’s portion.
It is distinct from cauls, the netted headdress of the women of Isaiah 3.
usage: The caul above the liver was the LORD’s, burnt upon the altar with the fat.
God claimed not the outward flesh only but the inmost and richest part.
As the caul was given whole to God, so must the hidden heart be laid upon the altar.

etymology: Kidney is of uncertain Middle English origin; fat is from Old English fætt, well-fed, rich. Together they render the Hebrew kelayoth (kidneys, seat of the affections) and heleb (the choice fat), the inward portions reserved as the LORD’s.
biblical_def: The two kidneys and the fat upon them were, by the law of the offerings, the LORD’s special portion, taken away and burnt upon the altar: “the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks” (Lev 3:4, 3:10). The fat was reckoned the best and richest of the beast, and the LORD claimed it as His own — “all the fat is the LORD’S” (Lev 3:16). The kidneys, deep-seated and hidden, were in Hebrew thought the seat of the affections and the secret reins that God alone tries and knows. So the very parts offered spoke of the innermost man. The prophets take up the figure in judgment and in blessing: the sword of the LORD is made fat “with the fat of the kidneys of rams” (Isa 34:6), and Israel was fed with “the fat of kidneys of wheat” (Deu 32:14), the choicest of the harvest. That the fat is the LORD’S teaches a great and abiding truth: God is worthy of the best and will not be put off with the lean and the leftover. To give Him the fat is to own that the richest of our substance, and the secret affections of our reins, belong wholly to Him. He who tries the reins asks the heart’s best; and He gave His own best, His only-begotten, that we might learn to withhold nothing.
webster_summary: The two kidneys and the choice fat upon them, reserved as the LORD’s portion in the offerings.
webster_full: KIDNEYS AND FAT, the inward organs and the rich fat about them, burnt upon the altar as the LORD’s portion.
The fat was accounted the best of the beast, and the law declared that all the fat is the LORD’s.
The kidneys were held to be the seat of the secret affections, the reins that God tries.
The prophets use the fat of kidneys as a figure of the choicest of a thing, whether of rams or of wheat.
The word fat is from Old English fætt, meaning rich or well-fed.

corruption_summary: A portion of the offering, not a contested doctrine; it recovers that the best and the inmost belong to the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The kidneys and the fat rebuke the man who brings God the lean and keeps the fat for himself. The age offers its leftovers to heaven and lavishes its richest upon its own pleasure; it gives God the thin edges of its time and treasure. But the law that burnt the fat upon the altar declares that the best is His by right, and that to withhold it is to rob Him of His portion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fat is the LORD’s. He is worthy of the choicest, and He tries the reins and the hidden affections. To give Him the fat and the kidneys is to yield Him both the richest of our substance and the secret of our hearts, withholding nothing from the God who withheld not His own Son.
roots_summary: The kidneys and the choice fat, the LORD’s portion, teaching that the best and inmost are His.
roots_lines: Kidneys and fat — the inward organs and rich fat burnt as the LORD’s portion (Lev 3:4).
The law declared that all the fat is the LORD’s (Lev 3:16).
The kidneys were held the seat of the affections, the reins that God tries.

The word fat is Old English fætt, rich or well-fed.
usage: The fat is the LORD’s; He will not be served with the lean and the leftover.
He who tries the reins asks for the heart’s best, not its remnants.
As the fat of kidneys was the choicest of the beast, so God claims the choicest of us.

etymology: From Old English inneweard, that which is within, rendering the Hebrew qereb, the inner part or midst. It names the entrails and inner organs of the sacrificial beast, which were washed with water and offered with the fat upon the altar.
biblical_def: The inwards were the inner parts — the entrails and viscera — of the beast brought to the altar, dealt with according to a careful rule in the law of the offerings. The fat that covered them was burnt to the LORD (Exo 29:13; Lev 3:3), and the inwards themselves, together with the legs, were washed with water before the whole was consumed: “But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar” (Lev 1:9). In the sin offering the bullock’s skin, flesh, head, legs, and inwards and dung were carried forth without the camp (Lev 4:11). Two things the inwards teach. First, that God lays open the inner man: the offering was not accepted with its inwards hidden and unwashed, but everything within was exposed, cleansed, and given up. Nothing secret was withheld from His eye. Second, that the whole man, and not the outward parts alone, must be sanctified; the inwards washed with water figure the cleansing of the conscience and the hidden thoughts. The LORD looketh not on the outward appearance but on the heart, and He will have the inner man laid bare before Him and purged. What water did to the inwards of the beast, the blood of Christ and the washing of the word do to the inward parts of His people, that they may be an offering of a sweet savour unto God.
webster_summary: The inner parts or entrails of a sacrificial beast, washed with water and offered upon the altar.
webster_full: INWARDS, the inner parts, entrails, or viscera of a beast offered in sacrifice.
The fat covering the inwards was burnt upon the altar as the LORD’s portion.
The inwards themselves, with the legs, were washed with water before being consumed.
In the sin offering the inwards were carried forth without the camp with the rest of the beast.
The word is from Old English inneweard, that which is within.

corruption_summary: A part of the offering, not a contested doctrine; it recovers that God lays open and cleanses the whole inner man.
corruption_paragraphs: The inwards rebuke a religion content with an outward show while the hidden parts remain unwashed. The age is careful of appearances and careless of the heart; it polishes the outside of the cup and leaves the within full of uncleanness. But the law that washed the inwards of the offering testifies that God will not accept a sacrifice whose inner parts are hidden and defiled.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the whole inner man must be laid open and cleansed before God. The inwards were washed with water and given wholly to the altar; so the conscience and the hidden thoughts must be purged by the blood of Christ and the washing of the word, that the worshipper may be an offering of a sweet savour.
roots_summary: The inner parts of the offering, washed and consumed, figuring the whole inner man laid open and cleansed before God.
roots_lines: Inwards — the entrails and inner parts of the sacrificial beast (Exo 29:13).
The inwards, with the legs, were washed with water before burning (Lev 1:9).
The fat that covered the inwards was burnt as the LORD’s portion (Lev 3:3).

The word is Old English inneweard, that which is within.
usage: The inwards were washed with water; nothing hidden was offered unclean to God.
The LORD looketh on the heart and will have the inner man laid open before Him.
As water cleansed the inwards, so the blood of Christ purges the conscience within.

etymology: Pot is from Old English pott, a vessel; the golden pot (Greek stamnos, in Hebrews) held an omer of manna (Hebrew man, “what is it?”). It names not the bread itself but the memorial vessel laid up before the LORD.
biblical_def: The pot of manna was a golden vessel, holding an omer of the wilderness bread, laid up before the LORD as a lasting memorial of His provision. At Moses’ command Aaron took “a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations” (Exo 16:33); and so “Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept” (Exo 16:34). In the sanctuary it was set within the ark, as Hebrews recounts of the holy place: “the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant” (Heb 9:4). It was a witness kept unspoiled, that generations who never gathered the daily bread might see how God had fed their fathers forty years in a barren land. The pot is distinct from the manna itself: the food fell and was eaten and bred worms if hoarded, but this portion, sealed in gold before the Testimony, did not corrupt. Herein it points to Christ, the true bread from heaven, laid up incorruptible for His people. The Lord promises to the overcomer “the hidden manna” (Rev 2:17) — a secret and everlasting nourishment, Christ Himself preserved and given, whom the world does not see, but on whom the church feeds forever within the veil.
webster_summary: The golden vessel holding an omer of manna, laid up before the Testimony as a memorial of God’s provision.
webster_full: POT OF MANNA, a golden vessel in which an omer of manna was preserved before the LORD.
It was laid up by Aaron at God’s command, to be kept for the generations of Israel.
It was placed within the ark of the covenant in the holy of holies.
It is distinct from manna as the daily food; it is the memorial portion, kept incorruptible.
The Epistle to the Hebrews names it the golden pot that had manna, wherein God’s provision was remembered.
scriptures: And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations.
As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept.
Heb 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
Rev 2:17

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
corruption_summary: A memorial vessel of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the incorruptible provision of Christ, the hidden manna laid up for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: The pot of manna rebukes a forgetful generation that lives on the day’s bread and remembers not the God who gave it. The manna gathered and hoarded bred worms; only the portion sealed before the LORD endured. The age fills its barns and forgets its Feeder, and so has no memorial of grace to hand down to its children. The golden pot stands against that forgetfulness, a kept witness of God’s faithful feeding.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ is the incorruptible bread laid up for His people. The manna that fell corrupted, but the pot’s portion, sealed in gold before the Testimony, did not; so the true bread from heaven is preserved unspoiled, the hidden manna given to the overcomer. It is distinct from the manna as daily food; this is the memorial kept forever.
roots_summary: The golden pot of preserved manna before the ark, memorial of God’s provision and figure of the incorruptible Christ.
roots_lines: Pot of manna — a golden vessel holding an omer of manna, laid up before the LORD (Exo 16:33).
Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept for the generations (Exo 16:34).
It was placed within the ark of the covenant in the holy place (Heb 9:4).
It is distinct from manna the daily food; this portion was kept incorruptible.
It figures the hidden manna, Christ preserved and given to the overcomer (Rev 2:17).
usage: The manna men hoarded bred worms, but the pot’s portion before the LORD did not corrupt.
The golden pot was a memorial, that children unborn might know how God fed their fathers.
Christ is the hidden manna, laid up incorruptible for all who overcome.

etymology: Wheel is from Old English hwēol, rendering the Hebrew ophan, a wheel or roller. It names the brazen wheels set beneath the ten wheeled bases that bore Solomon’s lavers, distinct from the single fixed laver of the tabernacle.
biblical_def: The wheels of the lavers were the brazen wheels wrought beneath the ten movable bases that carried the ten lavers of Solomon’s temple. Unlike the one fixed laver of the tabernacle, these were mounted upon wheeled carriages, that the vessels of washing might be moved about the court. Huram made them so: “every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass” (1Ki 7:30); the wheels ran under the borders, and “the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base” (1Ki 7:32). Their craftsmanship is set down with care: “the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” (1Ki 7:33), and all belonged to the ten bases of brass Solomon made (1Ki 7:27). The lavers held the water for washing the things that were offered; the wheels made that cleansing water to move throughout the court where the sacrifices were prepared. Herein is a quiet figure. The provision of cleansing in the house of God was not fixed to one spot only, but was carried near to every place of need. So the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness is not far off and immovable, but comes to the sinner where he is; the water of purifying is brought to the very place of the labour and the blood. Even the wheels of brass, made like a chariot’s, preach that God’s cleansing runs to meet His people.
webster_summary: The brazen wheels beneath the ten movable bases that bore the lavers of Solomon’s temple.
webster_full: WHEELS OF THE LAVERS, the brasen wheels set under the wheeled bases of Solomon’s ten lavers.
Each base had four wheels of brass with plates and undersetters.
The axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base, and ran beneath its borders.
The work of the wheels was fashioned like the work of a chariot wheel, all of molten brass.
They belong to the movable lavers of the temple, distinct from the one fixed laver of the tabernacle.
scriptures: And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.
And under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten.
And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it.
corruption_summary: A furnishing of the temple, not a contested doctrine; it recovers that God’s cleansing is carried near to His people where they labour.
corruption_paragraphs: The wheels of the lavers rebuke the thought that the means of cleansing are distant and hard to reach. The age imagines God far off and His purifying beyond its labour, and so leaves its uncleanness unwashed. But the wheeled lavers testify that in the house of God the water of washing was made to move throughout the court, brought near to every place where the offering was prepared.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fountain of cleansing comes near to the sinner. The lavers ran upon wheels like a chariot’s, that the purifying water might reach the place of the blood and the labour. So the cleansing opened in Christ is not immovable and far off, but is brought to His people where they stand in their need. These wheeled bases are distinct from the single fixed laver of the tabernacle.
roots_summary: The chariot-like brazen wheels of Solomon’s movable lavers, figuring cleansing brought near to God’s people.

The axletrees were joined to the base, the wheels running beneath its borders (1Ki 7:32).
They were fashioned like a chariot wheel, with naves, felloes, and spokes, all molten (1Ki 7:33).
They bore the lavers of washing about the court of Solomon’s temple.
They are distinct from the single fixed laver of the tabernacle.
usage: The lavers ran upon wheels, that the cleansing water might reach every place of the offering.
As the wheels carried the washing near, so God’s purifying comes to the sinner where he stands.
Even the brazen wheels, made like a chariot’s, preach a cleansing that runs to meet His people.

etymology: Base is from the Greek basis, a foundation or pedestal, rendering the Hebrew mekonah, a fixed stand or wheeled support. It names the ten brazen carriages that upheld and bore the lavers of Solomon’s temple.
biblical_def: The bases of the lavers were the ten wheeled stands of brass that Huram made to bear the ten lavers of Solomon’s temple: “he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it” (1Ki 7:27). Upon each was set one laver: “upon every one of the ten bases one laver” (1Ki 7:38), and together they are numbered among the vessels Huram wrought, “the ten bases, and ten lavers on the bases” (1Ki 7:43). They were adorned carriages of brass, panelled with lions, oxen, and cherubims, and set upon wheels, that the lavers of washing might be upheld and moved about the court. Long after, wicked king Ahaz laid impious hands upon them: he “cut off the borders of the bases, and removed the laver from off them” (2Ki 16:17), stripping the house of God to serve the king of Assyria. Two lessons stand together. The base bore the laver: the cleansing vessel did not float unsupported but rested upon a firm and appointed foundation; so the ordinances of washing in God’s house are set upon His own institution, not upon the fancy of men. And Ahaz’s sacrilege warns how quickly an unbelieving heart will deface and dismantle what God has ordained. These wheeled bases are distinct from the tabernacle’s single fixed laver; they are Solomon’s ten brazen stands.
webster_summary: The ten wheeled brazen stands that upheld and bore the lavers of Solomon’s temple.
webster_full: BASES OF THE LAVERS, the ten movable stands of brass on which the lavers of Solomon’s temple rested.
Each base was four cubits square and three cubits high, wrought of cast brass.
They were panelled with lions, oxen, and cherubims, and set upon wheels.
Upon each base stood one laver, ten lavers in all.
King Ahaz cut off their borders and removed the lavers from them in his sacrilege.
scriptures: And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it.
Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths: and every laver was four cubits: and upon every one of the ten bases one laver.
And the ten bases, and ten lavers on the bases;
And king Ahaz cut off the borders of the bases, and removed the laver from off them; and took down the sea from off the brasen oxen that were under it, and put it upon a pavement of stones.
corruption_summary: A furnishing of the temple, not a contested doctrine; it recovers that God’s ordinances of cleansing rest upon His own appointed foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: The bases of the lavers rebuke the presumption that would remove and deface what God has set in His house. Ahaz cut off their borders and took the lavers from off them to purchase the favour of Assyria; and the age still dismantles God’s ordinances to serve its own conveniences and its idols. Whatever the unbelieving heart cannot use for itself, it strips and carries away.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the vessels of cleansing rest upon an appointed foundation, not upon the will of men. The laver stood upon its base by God’s pattern; and where men, like Ahaz, tear away that foundation, worship is defaced. These bases are distinct from the single fixed laver of the tabernacle; they are Solomon’s ten brazen stands.
roots_summary: The ten wheeled brazen stands that bore Solomon’s lavers, teaching that cleansing rests on God’s appointed foundation.
